summary: Reports on a 2014 London workshop about domain name collisions, which happen when a name used privately collides with one that later appears in the public DNS. It summarizes the discussion of causes and possible mitigations. It is an informational report, not a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine two kids in different towns both named their pet Max, and then the towns merge. This report is a meeting where experts talked about what goes wrong when names clash and how to avoid it.

questions: how does icann manage name collisions
subtitle: Workshop findings on domain name collisions when new TLDs clash with private networks.

tldr.problem: When ICANN adds new top-level domains to the public DNS root, they can collide with names that organizations have used privately, causing systems to resolve to unexpected destinations and breaking services.
tldr.mechanism: The document reports on a 2014 workshop where researchers and operators discussed the causes of name collisions, how to measure them, and mitigation strategies including controlled interruption and monitoring of root traffic.
tldr.outcome: ICANN adopted a collision occurrence management framework that includes delayed delegation for risky names, blocking of second-level domains in new TLDs, and public education efforts to help organizations migrate away from colliding namespaces.

today: RFC 8023 is an informational report on the 2014 workshop and is not a protocol specification. ICANN has since adopted the Name Collision Occurrence Management Framework discussed at the workshop. The document serves as a historical record of the community's response to the new gTLD program and the associated collision risks.

sections.title: What Are Domain Name Collisions?
sections.content:
A name collision occurs when a name used in a private network (like an internal company intranet) collides with a new top-level domain (TLD) registered in the public DNS root. For example, an organization might use the name "corp" internally to refer to their corporate network, but if ".corp" becomes a registered TLD, DNS queries from that organization's systems could unexpectedly reach the public Internet instead of the private server.

Before 2013, there were only a small number of TLDs in the DNS root (such as .com, .org, .edu). Many organizations confidently used non-delegated names like ".local", ".internal", ".home", or ".corp" for their internal networks, believing there was no risk of collision. However, ICANN's new gTLD program opened the possibility of hundreds or thousands of new TLDs being delegated. This created a significant risk: systems using these previously-safe names could suddenly resolve to public Internet destinations, potentially exposing sensitive internal traffic or breaking service discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: Companies used fake names they made up (like "sales.internal") thinking nobody on the real Internet would ever use them. But then the real Internet started using those same names, and things broke.

sections.title: Background and Context
sections.content:
The document provides historical context on the escalation of this issue. In 2008, the Internet Architecture Board warned that new TLD additions could cause instability. By December 2010, the Security and Stability Advisory Committee (SSAC) published reports on root scaling. In May 2013, ICANN commissioned a study by the Interisle Consulting Group that analyzed DNS traffic and identified categories of risk: 80% of applied-for TLD strings were low-risk, 20% had uncalculated risk, and 2 strings (.home and .corp) were classified as high-risk due to widespread internal use.

ICANN responded with a "New gTLD Collision Occurrence Management Plan" in August 2013. This plan included options for delaying high-risk TLDs indefinitely, temporarily delaying medium-risk ones for 2-3 months, and blocking second-level domains in new TLDs for 120 days after delegation. Many applicants elected an "alternative path to delegation" in which they would proceed with delegation but initially block all second-level domains found in DNS traffic datasets.
sections.plainLanguage: Experts studied the problem and found that out of hundreds of new names being requested, only a few were really risky. They came up with a plan to delay those risky ones or block queries to them for a while.

sections.title: Workshop Structure and Research Findings
sections.content:
The workshop took place March 8-10, 2014 in London, bringing together subject-area specialists, researchers, and TLD operators. It was sponsored by Verisign and included peer-reviewed papers, invited talks, and panel discussions.

Research presentations analyzed DNS traffic data from "Day in the Life of the Internet" (DITL) datasets to understand collision patterns. Speakers examined the effectiveness of blocking lists created from sampled DNS data, finding that such lists were less effective than expected at preventing actual collisions. Other research measured the use of DNS recursion-desired (RD) bits in root queries, analyzed search lists in resolver configurations, and created models to quantify collision risk from first principles by studying how client name resolution libraries behave.

A key finding was that the DITL dataset, while widely used as a reference, had potential bias issues after the ICANN "Reveal Day" when applied-for gTLD strings were publicly announced. Presenters also emphasized that the analysis of interactions between local and global DNS namespaces was an under-researched area, and that better shared data collection and monitoring infrastructure was needed across the community.
sections.plainLanguage: Experts presented research on how often these problems actually happen and tested different ways to prevent them. They found that while some solutions looked good on paper, they did not work perfectly in real networks.

sections.title: Proposed Mitigation Strategies
sections.content:
The workshop covered several mitigation approaches. At the ICANN level, the main strategy discussed was "controlled interruption," in which a registry would temporarily resolve all second-level domains (or all SLDs present in a block list) to a specific address (127.0.53.53). This allows operators to detect the collision and reconfigure their systems, while minimizing long-term disruption.

Other proposed mitigations applied at the enterprise level. Organizations were advised to educate administrators and users about collisions, implement monitoring to detect collisions when they occur, and proactively migrate from non-delegated namespaces to reserved namespaces like those defined in RFC 6761 (such as ".local", ".test", or ".example"). The workshop emphasized the importance of outreach and education, comparing name collision transitions to how the postal and telephone systems have historically managed major addressing changes.

Participants agreed that a lack of tools, shared data, and communication had hampered the ability of operators to measure and proactively address collisions. The consensus was that future work should focus on improved monitoring, data collection, and communication between ICANN, registries, and operators.
sections.plainLanguage: Solutions included temporarily redirecting queries to a special address so people notice and fix their systems, and helping companies switch from fake names to safe ones that are reserved just for that purpose.

sections.title: Conclusions and Next Steps
sections.content:
The workshop program committee concluded that analysis of interactions between local and global DNS namespaces remained a "nonexistent topic of research" due to lack of accessible data, lack of established theory, and participation bias. Attendees reaffirmed the need to understand the root causes of name collisions and to overcome shortcomings in shared data collection and DNS monitoring.

Key unknowns remained: What are the actual root causes of collision-inducing queries? What happens inside recursive name servers when collisions occur? What new vulnerabilities or attack vectors do colliding TLDs enable? Without sufficient datasets and funding for data collection and analysis, the community was making inferences and "rank guesses" rather than addressing the problem systematically.

In the time following the workshop (noted in a brief update), ICANN finalized its Name Collision Occurrence Management Framework in July 2014, and published management documents for implementing controlled interruption. RSSAC published a specification for common measurements that root operators would collect. However, broad community efforts to measure collision impact were not included in the final recommendation, leaving open questions about the actual real-world effect of the mitigations.
sections.plainLanguage: The workshop showed that while the community had ideas for solutions, there were still many unanswered questions about why these problems happen and how bad they really are.
